title: Rockets
objective: After this level you can explain how rockets push themselves forward in the vacuum of space.
summary: A rocket pushes on its own exhaust, not on air, and carries its own oxidizer, so it works in a vacuum. Goddard flew the first liquid-fueled rocket in 1926.

cards.headline: In 1920, a newspaper said rockets could never work in space.
cards.body: The New York Times mocked rocket pioneer Robert Goddard, claiming a rocket in a vacuum would have nothing to push against. On July 17, 1969, with Apollo 11 on its way to the Moon, the paper printed a correction. Who was right says a lot about how rockets work.

cards.headline: It pushes on its own exhaust
cards.body: The Times had Level 32's law backwards. A rocket burns its propellant, and the nozzle accelerates the hot exhaust out of the back. By Newton's third law, the exhaust pushes back on the rocket, and that reaction is the thrust. Nothing outside is needed: the rocket isn't pushing on air or on the launch pad. It's pushing on its own exhaust, which works just as well in a vacuum.

cards.headline: Why a jet can't follow it up
cards.body: Burning needs an oxidizer. A jet engine takes its oxygen from the air around it, so where there's no air, it can't work. A rocket carries its oxidizer on board along with its fuel. In a liquid rocket, both are pumped into a combustion chamber, where they mix and burn. That's why a rocket works in space and a jet engine doesn't. It brings its own breath, in a sense.

cards.fact: The first liquid-fueled rocket flew for just 2.5 seconds.
cards.context: On March 16, 1926, on a farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, Goddard launched a rocket burning gasoline and liquid oxygen. It rose 41 feet and landed 184 feet away. Not a long trip, but it was the first flight of a rocket burning liquid fuel with oxygen it carried along.

questions.prompt: How can a rocket burn its fuel in space, where there is no air?

options.label: Its fuel burns without any oxidizer
It scoops gas from space as it flies
options.rationale: There is essentially nothing to scoop.

questions.explanation: A rocket carries its oxidizer on board with its fuel, so it can burn and make thrust in a vacuum.

questions.prompt: The Times's 1920 editorial said a rocket in a vacuum has nothing to push against. What does a rocket actually push against?

options.label: The air around it
options.rationale: There is no air in space, and it still works.

options.label: The launch pad
options.rationale: It keeps accelerating long after leaving the pad.

options.label: Earth's magnetic field
options.rationale: Magnetism plays no part in rocket thrust.

questions.explanation: The rocket throws its exhaust backward, and the exhaust pushes the rocket forward: action and reaction.

questions.prompt: Level 32's jet engine and a rocket both throw hot gas backward. Why can't the jet work in space?

options.label: It takes its oxygen from the surrounding air
Its turbine freezes in the cold
Jet fuel doesn't burn in darkness
It is too heavy to reach space
options.rationale: Weight isn't the reason it can't run there.

questions.explanation: A jet engine gets its oxygen from the air; with no air there is nothing to burn with, while a rocket carries its own oxidizer.
